generalizedRange: Luzon, Samar, Leyte, and Mindanao, the Philippines
hook: One eagle needs a forest bigger than Manhattan.

story.text: The Philippine eagle wears a crest of long feathers that flares into a shaggy mane around pale grey-blue eyes — a face unlike any other eagle's.
It is one of the largest and most powerful forest raptors: a metre of bird with a six-and-a-half-foot wingspan, flying fast through dense trees.
It hunts the canopy — civets, flying squirrels, snakes, even other raptors — sometimes in pairs, one bird distracting while the other strikes.
Everything about it is slow: a single egg every two years, and a chick that stays with its parents for nearly two more.
One pair needs four to eleven thousand hectares of forest — so every eagle lost usually means a forest lost first.
It survives on four islands and nowhere else on Earth, and it is the national bird of the Philippines.
The threats are the chainsaw and the gun: deforestation, and at least one eagle shot every year despite protection.
The answer is patient and local: the Philippine Eagle Center breeds and rehabilitates eagles in Davao, and Indigenous forest guards patrol the nesting forests.
Released eagles now fly with GPS trackers — trained first to avoid the power poles that could kill them.
To witness the Philippine eagle is to hold four islands' forests in one gaze.

reproduction.text: A single egg every two years, incubated about sixty days. The chick fledges at four to five months but depends on its parents for up to seventeen more — and will not breed until it is five to seven years old.

insight.text: A single Philippine eagle needs at least 7,000 hectares of forest to thrive — more land than Manhattan, for one bird.
